AH-001.title: The Archer King
AH-001.historical_description: This coin depicts the iconic Achaemenid archer king — a motif that defined Persian royal coinage for over two centuries.
AH-001.story: Legend says Cyrus the Great never lost a battle. His arrows, like his will, always found their mark.

AH-002.title: The Lion and the Bull
AH-002.historical_description: The eternal struggle between lion and bull is one of the most powerful symbols in ancient Persian art.
AH-002.story: At Nowruz, the sun rises and the lion conquers the bull — light defeats darkness. This coin captures that eternal moment.

AH-003.title: The Winged Bull
AH-003.historical_description: The Lamassu — a celestial guardian with the body of a bull and the wings of an eagle — stood at the gates of Achaemenid palaces.
AH-003.story: They say a guardian spirit never sleeps. The winged bull watched over Persepolis for centuries, long after the empire had turned to dust.

AH-004.title: The Faravahar of Pasargadae
AH-004.historical_description: The four-winged Faravahar carved at Pasargadae is the oldest known representation of this sacred symbol. It stands as the purest expression of Achaemenid spiritual power.
AH-004.story: In Zoroastrian belief, the Faravahar is the eternal guardian spirit — present before birth, watchful during life, and enduring beyond death.

AH-005.title: Portrait of the King
AH-005.historical_description: The profile portrait of the bearded Persian king became the definitive image of Achaemenid power. The king's gaze toward the horizon symbolizes foresight and sovereignty.
AH-005.story: Cyrus was called Father by his people — not a conqueror, but a liberator. His face on a coin was a promise: of justice, of peace, of civilization.

AH-006.title: Tomb of Cyrus Under the Stars
AH-006.historical_description: The tomb of Cyrus the Great at Pasargadae has stood for 2,500 years — a monument to the man who authored the world's first human rights charter.
AH-006.story: When Alexander the Great visited the tomb, he found the inscription: O man, whoever you are — I am Cyrus, who gave the Persians their empire. Do not begrudge me this little earth that covers my body.
